title: Using brain wave recordings to detect and monitor delirium in older hospitalised patients
official: The Delirium Electroencephalography and Phenotyping with Endpoints (DEPEND) study
summary:
Background and study aims
Delirium is a condition of sudden confusion and changes in awareness, affecting around 1 in 4 older patients in hospital at any given time, usually when someone is unwell for another reason. Delirium is very serious. It is linked to longer hospital stays, long-term memory problems, and an increased risk of death. However, it often goes unrecognised by healthcare professionals. At present, doctors and nurses assess delirium using bedside behavioural tests. These can be subjective and hard to interpret, particularly in patients who already have conditions such as dementia.
Electroencephalography (EEG) safely records the brain’s electrical activity through the scalp, and could help detect delirium. However, traditional EEG needs expensive equipment, along with specialists to record and then interpret the signals. In the NHS, EEG is poorly available and there are not enough specialists. Newer portable EEG equipment is much easier to use, and can be fitted at the bedside by non-specialist staff.
This study aims to combine portable EEG with computer analysis to develop an automated, objective bedside measure of delirium. The goal is provide simple numbers describing brain function, similar to how a blood pressure reading gives a simple number describing the circulation.

Who can participate?
The study is open to:
1. Adults aged 65 years and over who are currently in hospital, expected to stay longer than 24 hours, who may or may not have delirium
2. Healthy adults aged 65 years and over living in the community, with no history of delirium, dementia, or other significant neurological or psychiatric conditions.
Delirium can affect a person’s ability to make decisions about taking part. Patients in this situation can still join the study, provided a consultee – usually a relative or close friend who knows them well – agrees that taking part is in keeping with their wishes and feelings.
Participants may also be asked to name an informant: a partner, relative or close friend, ideally someone who has known them for 10 years or more, who can answer some questions about them. Having an informant is helpful but is not required to take part.
People cannot take part if they are on a ventilator, if their confusion is due to alcohol withdrawal, if they have severe scalp skin problems that would prevent an EEG recording, or if they are unable to consent and no consultee is available.

What does the study involve?
Participants take part in up to four types of assessment over about a year.
1. Baseline assessment (during the hospital admission, or at Imperial College London for healthy volunteers): a brain wave recording using a portable EEG headset, computerised memory and thinking tests done on a tablet or computer, a blood sample, and a clinical interview and examination. Hospitalised participants are also asked to wear a smartwatch, and to have a sleep sensor placed under the mattress and a small environmental sensor placed nearby.
2. Repeat assessments (hospitalised participants only): up to five shorter visits, about every 1 to 3 days during the hospital stay, including a portable EEG recording, a clinical examination, and thinking tests.
3. Follow-up assessment (about 6 months after discharge, or after the baseline visit for healthy volunteers): similar to the baseline assessment but without the standard clinical EEG. This can take place at the hospital, at Imperial College London, or at the participant’s home.
4. Remote follow-up (about 12 months after discharge or baseline): by telephone or video call, including a short interview and computerised thinking tests.
The blood samples are taken in the same way as a routine hospital blood test. They are tested for markers of inflammation, of injury to nerve cells, and of neurodegeneration, and for genes involved in brain function, repair and neurodegeneration. 
All assessments are carried out by trained members of the research team. Taking part is entirely voluntary, and it does not affect a participant’s clinical care in any way.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants will not receive any direct medical benefit from taking part. The study may, however, lead to better tools for detecting and monitoring delirium in older hospital patients in future, which could benefit a great many people.
The risks of taking part are minimal. The portable EEG headset is non-invasive and painless, although the electrodes can occasionally feel slightly uncomfortable. The blood sample involves a small needle prick and can cause minor bruising.

Where is the study run from?
The study is sponsored by Imperial College London. It takes place across three Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust hospitals: Charing Cross Hospital, Hammersmith Hospital, and St Mary’s Hospital, all in London, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to April 2030

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Gregory Scott, gregory.scott99@imperial.ac.uk

interventions.name:
This is a longitudinal observational study that involves assessing participants at multiple time points. It does not involve any invasive procedures and it will not interfere with the clinical care of participants.

The study is in people ≥65 years old, also called older people.

The following group

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
For hospitalised patients (groups a-b):
1. Age >=65 years 
2. Clinically likely to be admitted for >24 hours
3. Able to consent or an available consultee

For healthy participants (group c):
1. Age >=65 years
2. No history of delirium, dementia, or other significant neurological or psychiatric disorder
Exclusion criteria:
For all participants (groups a-c):
1. Intubated
2. Delirium due to alcohol withdrawal
3. Unwillingness or anticipated inability to follow all the study procedures
4. Severe scalp skin lesions (e.g., extensive broken skin) that would preclude EEG
5. Lacking capacity to consent and no available consultee
6. Any other medical or psychiatric condition or any treatment which, in the opinion of the investigators, would interfere with the study or compromise patient safety
